CVP-A18:0.title: Trace the ventral foregut outgrowth
body: Start with a single foregut tube. In week 4 an endoderm-lined groove on its ventral wall evaginates as the laryngotracheal diverticulum. The proximal connection remains at the laryngeal inlet, allowing the airway to open into the pharynx. The dorsal foregut continues as the esophagus. On a sagittal drawing, establish ventral and dorsal before naming either lumen.

Follow the endodermal lining from the foregut into the new bud. It becomes respiratory epithelium and its glands, including the distal alveolar epithelium. The splanchnic mesoderm surrounding that tube forms the supporting connective tissue, cartilage and smooth muscle of the developing tracheobronchial system. A defect confined to epithelial differentiation therefore points to a different tissue lineage than one affecting the surrounding cartilage.
CVP-A18:0.example: In an unlabeled section, an epithelial-lined ventral bud surrounded by mesenchyme contains both germ-layer contributions. Identify the lining and supporting wall separately.

CVP-A18:1.title: Map branches to adult lobes and segments
body: The distal lung bud divides into right and left primary bronchial buds. Each primary bud forms the main bronchus of one lung. Secondary (lobar) branches supply lobes, so count three on the right and two on the left. Tertiary (segmental) branches supply bronchopulmonary segments within those lobes. In a branching tree, identify the level by the territory supplied instead of by how large the branch looks.

Successive branching generates conducting airways that deliver air to the developing distal lung. Formation of a lobar or segmental bronchus establishes the map of its territory before the terminal units develop a thin, vascular exchange interface. The presence of an orderly airway tree is therefore insufficient evidence that the lung can exchange gases.
CVP-A18:1.example: Trace one right-sided branch in the course figure from main bronchus to a lobar branch, then to a segmental branch. The three right lobar branches do not imply three right bronchopulmonary segments.

CVP-A18:2.title: Read the four developmental stages in order
body: During the pseudoglandular stage (roughly 6–16 weeks in this deck), branching creates a gland-like appearance, chiefly reflecting conducting airways. In the canalicular stage (16–26 weeks), the distal lumina enlarge and vascularity increases. This brings future exchange epithelium and capillaries closer together. Ask what anatomical change is happening before memorizing a week boundary.

During the terminal-sac stage (approximately 26 weeks to birth in the course slide), distal sacs expand and the exchange barrier becomes thinner. Alveolar development overlaps this phase, beginning around 32 weeks in the lecture timeline and continuing after birth as septation creates more units. Exact childhood endpoints differ within the slides; the stable takeaway is that birth is followed by substantial maturation.
Type I cells form the thin exchange surface; type II cells secrete surfactant. This distinction connects the morphological stages to gas exchange and distal stability.
CVP-A18:2.example: A specimen with branching tubes but little capillary contact fits earlier development than one with expanded thin-walled terminal sacs. Do not infer viability from the stage name alone.

CVP-A18:resp26-origin.title: Separate airway and esophagus during development
body: The week 4 outgrowth is lined by foregut endoderm, which becomes airway epithelium; its surrounding splanchnic mesoderm provides supporting tissue.

The initial diverticulum shares a lumen with the foregut. Tracheoesophageal folds grow toward the midline and unite to separate a ventral laryngotracheal tube from the dorsal esophagus. The cranial communication at the laryngeal inlet remains useful. A connection between the distal trachea and esophagus is abnormal.

Compare the variants in the lecture panels. In isolated atresia the esophageal tube has no continuous passage. In isolated fistula an abnormal connection can exist even if the esophagus remains continuous. A common combination is proximal esophageal atresia with a distal fistula opening into the airway. Follow each lumen independently in the figure, since the blind proximal pouch and distal communicating segment explain different findings.
CVP-A18:resp26-origin.example: If a feeding tube stops in a proximal pouch and the stomach contains air, the pouch explains tube obstruction and a distal connection can explain air in the stomach. Pure atresia without a distal connection does not provide that airway route.

CVP-A18:resp26-maturation.title: Connect type I and II cells to neonatal breathing
body: Type I alveolar cells are thin and spread across the gas-exchange surface. Close apposition to capillaries shortens the diffusion path. Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant into the lining fluid. Its action at the air–liquid interface lowers surface tension, which helps stabilize distal units as they become smaller during expiration.

When surfactant is inadequate, distal units are more liable to collapse and more pressure is needed to reopen them. This lowers compliance and increases the work of inflation. Distinguish that mechanism from reduced lung size after chronic compression. Both can present with respiratory distress, but one principally concerns surface forces and the other concerns the amount of lung that formed.

Use the stage sequence as a comparison: pseudoglandular branching precedes canalicular enlargement and vascular association, followed by terminal sacs. About 28 weeks falls in the terminal-sac period in the course timeline.
CVP-A18:resp26-maturation.example: Compare two infants with respiratory distress. A very premature infant may have immature type II function, while an infant with a large congenital diaphragmatic defect may have a compressed, hypoplastic lung.

CVP-A18:resp26-cavities.title: Follow the coelom into separate pleural cavities
body: Embryonic folding brings the lateral edges ventrally and helps bring the intraembryonic coelom inside the body. The growing bronchial buds expand into the pericardioperitoneal canals alongside the foregut. The layer over the growing lung becomes visceral pleura from splanchnic mesoderm. The body-wall-facing layer becomes parietal pleura from somatic mesoderm. The pleural cavity lies between these layers.

Read the cross-sections from early canals to separated cavities. Pleuropericardial folds grow between the expanding pleural space and the central pericardial space. These folds carry the phrenic nerves and common cardinal veins in the early diagram. As the membranes complete separation, they contribute to fibrous pericardium. Pleuroperitoneal folds instead close the connection toward the abdomen.
CVP-A18:resp26-cavities.example: On an axial drawing with the heart in the midline, name the membrane separating the heart cavity from a lateral lung cavity, then distinguish it from the caudal closure separating thorax and abdomen.

CVP-A18:resp26-clinical.title: Explain pulmonary hypoplasia and interpret source cautions
body: Growth of the fetal lung requires room to expand, adequate fluid-related distension and fetal breathing movements. Oligohydramnios, as illustrated with fetal renal disease, is associated with restricted lung development. With diaphragmatic herniation, viscera crowd the thorax and physically restrict lung growth. In that setting the usual term is hypoplasia, meaning the lung forms but is underdeveloped. Agenesis means it never formed.

Compare growth restriction, surfactant deficiency and abnormal septation. A small compressed lung points to hypoplasia, expiratory instability in an immature lung points toward deficient surfactant, and airway contamination during feeding can follow a tracheoesophageal communication. The deck's gestational-age and flotation examples are historical simplifications. Lung flotation is affected by several factors and cannot establish live birth by itself, and clinical viability cannot be determined from one week threshold.
CVP-A18:resp26-clinical.example: In a fetus with severe oligohydramnios and small lungs, explain how the fetal environment altered growth even though the original respiratory diverticulum formed.

questions.question: A newborn’s feeding tube coils in a blind upper pouch. Abdominal imaging still shows gas in the stomach. What accounts for both findings?
options: Proximal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
An isolated fistula with a continuous esophagus
reasons: The blind upper pouch stops the tube. The distal fistula provides a route for tracheal air to reach the stomach.
A continuous esophagus lacks the blind proximal pouch in this case.
A blind pouch explains the tube, but isolated atresia does not provide an airway-to-stomach route.
It connects serous cavities, not the airway and distal digestive lumen.
questions.explanation: The blind upper pouch stops the tube. The distal fistula provides a route for tracheal air to reach the stomach.

CVP-A19:0.title: Trace the pleural lining around the root
body: Visceral pleura is applied to the lung and follows its lobes into the fissures. Parietal pleura lines the enclosing thoracic wall. It is named by the surface it faces: costal over the rib cage, diaphragmatic over the diaphragm, mediastinal beside the mediastinum, and cervical where it extends into the root of the neck. These are regions of one continuous parietal lining.

Trace the visceral sheet toward the root and follow its reflection onto the mediastinum. The two sheets can glide because a thin film of serous fluid lubricates their apposed surfaces. The fluid interface also helps maintain mechanical coupling between chest wall and lung. A fissure between lobes is lined by visceral pleura on both sides; it is not a costal reflection.
CVP-A19:0.example: In a dissection image, identify the layer covering the exposed lung and the layer lining the adjacent rib cage. Then find where continuity is restored near the root.

CVP-A19:1.title: Separate pleural pain from stretch sensation
body: Parietal pleura responds to somatic pain, touch, pressure and temperature. Visceral pleura receives autonomic supply through the pulmonary plexus and can sense stretch, but it is relatively insensitive to the ordinary painful stimuli that sharply localize on the chest wall. Breathing moves the lung relative to the wall, which can aggravate pain when parietal pleura is inflamed.

The pathway follows the parietal region affected. Costal pleura and peripheral diaphragmatic pleura send pain via the intercostal nerves, tending to produce local chest-wall or lower thoracic pain. Mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura send sensory signals through the phrenic nerve. Distinguish the sensory route from phrenic motor supply to diaphragm muscle.
CVP-A19:1.example: Sharp pain at the irritated rib-level region during inspiration points to costal parietal pleura. A lung-surface stretch stimulus alone does not explain the same sharply localized somatic pain.

CVP-A19:2.title: Read a recess as space available for expansion
body: At the inferior reflection, the costal parietal sheet turns onto the diaphragm. Below the resting lung border the costal and diaphragmatic parietal surfaces oppose one another. This costodiaphragmatic recess is a potential extension of the pleural cavity. During deeper inspiration the descending lung margin occupies more of it; the recess itself is not a permanent compartment filled with lung.

In an upright person pleural fluid can settle into the dependent costodiaphragmatic recess. In the anterior chest a separate costomediastinal recess lies where the costal and mediastinal pleura meet. The cardiac notch makes this relationship more prominent on the left. A pleural recess is formed by reflections of parietal pleura, while a pulmonary fissure subdivides lung tissue.
CVP-A19:2.example: Use the lower-border figure to mark the lung edge first and then the pleural reflection. The band between them is a recess, so label neither boundary as the recess itself.

CVP-A19:resp26-surface.title: Project lung borders, fissures and listening areas
body: The apex rises about 2.5 cm above the clavicle into the neck, alongside the cervical pleural cupula. For the lower lung edge, remember ribs 6, 8 and 10 at midclavicular, midaxillary and posterior landmarks respectively. The pleural reflection reaches ribs 8, 10 and 12 at corresponding landmarks. These are approximate surface projections; breathing changes how far the lung extends into the recess.

The oblique fissure runs from near T2 posteriorly toward the sixth costal cartilage anteriorly on the course diagram. The right horizontal fissure follows the fourth costal cartilage to meet the oblique fissure. This places the right middle lobe mainly anteriorly and laterally between ribs 4 and 6. Upper lobes dominate the upper anterior chest, while much of the lower lobes lies posteriorly. The posterior chest therefore samples lower lobes more directly than the upper anterior chest.
CVP-A19:resp26-surface.example: At the midaxillary line the resting lower lung edge is near rib 8 and the pleural reflection near rib 10. Give both boundaries before naming the recess between them.

CVP-A19:resp26-layers.title: Predict where fluid, air and expanding lung go
body: The moving sheet is visceral pleura and extends into fissures. The stationary wall lining is parietal pleura; its mediastinal region covers the lateral face of the mediastinum.

Picture a lung covering that moves with the lung and a wall lining that stays with the thorax. With inspiration, the lung expands toward the lower parietal reflection, taking up space in the recess. Free pleural fluid instead follows gravity and can accumulate at the dependent base in an upright person. Fluid between the pleural sheets can compress adjacent lung without occupying its alveoli.

On an upright image, fluid in the dependent recess can blunt the normally sharp costophrenic angle. That angle is a projection of the lateral costal–diaphragmatic relationship. Contrast an effusion with air in the pleural space: both can reduce available expansion, but air and fluid distribute differently with position. Do not equate an abnormal costophrenic angle with inflammation alone.
CVP-A19:resp26-layers.example: Use the recess crop to explain why a dependent effusion can appear at the base while breath sounds from the lower lobe are generally best assessed posteriorly.

CVP-A19:resp26-sensory.title: Work out where pleural pain will be felt
body: Map the tissue before predicting referral. Costal parietal pleura and the diaphragm's peripheral pleura are innervated by intercostal nerves. Pain is generally felt in their own thoracic territories. Mediastinal and central diaphragmatic parietal pleura use phrenic afferents from C3–C5.

Phrenic afferents enter cervical segments that also receive somatic input from the shoulder region. Convergence can make central diaphragmatic irritation feel as if it comes from the shoulder. Compare this cervical pathway with cardiac pain referral to the medial arm through upper thoracic levels in A21. Both involve convergence, but the incoming nerves and segmental territories differ.
CVP-A19:resp26-sensory.example: If discomfort over the shoulder accompanies irritation over the central diaphragm, trace the path from parietal pleura through the phrenic nerve to cervical spinal segments.

CVP-A19:resp26-clinical.title: Distinguish pneumothorax, pleurisy and effusion
body: In pneumothorax, pleural air breaks the normal pressure relationship that keeps the lung expanded against the chest wall. The affected lung recoils. In the open example a chest-wall opening communicates with the exterior and air moves with breathing. Tension physiology requires pressure trapping and can impair venous return; an open wound and a tension mechanism are not interchangeable labels.

Pleurisy describes inflammation of the pleura. Inflamed surfaces can rub during breathing, producing pleuritic pain and a friction rub. A pleural effusion is fluid accumulation and can coexist with inflammation, although either can occur without the other. The cervical pleural cupula also explains why a misplaced approach near the subclavian region can enter the pleural space.

Thoracentesis concerns access to the pleural space, not lung parenchyma. For anatomy, the main intercostal bundle lies in the groove under the rib above, so explain the reasoning behind approaching just above the rib below. For clinical care, real access is selected using ultrasound and local protocols; the course slide’s landmark example is not a universal procedural instruction.
CVP-A19:resp26-clinical.example: When a case describes a chest-wall wound with free air movement, identify the mechanism. When it describes fluid in the dependent costophrenic recess, identify the compartment and explain why fluid can compress the lung.

CVP-A20:0.title: Map embryonic components to adult regions
body: The diaphragm has four classical embryologic contributors. The septum transversum contributes the central tendon, while the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus forms the crura. Pleuroperitoneal folds close the posterolateral canals and contribute to the partition. Peripheral muscular ingrowth from the body wall completes the muscular rim.

Use a section through the lower thorax to assign each contribution spatially. The central tendon occupies the noncontractile aponeurotic region. The crura anchor posteriorly and are adjacent to the esophageal route. The posterolateral folds fill the openings between the early thoracic and abdominal spaces. The surrounding body wall supplies the expanding peripheral muscular component. Naming the four pieces is only the first step; trace where they meet.
CVP-A20:0.example: If a question names the crus beside the esophagus, retrieve the dorsal esophageal mesentery. If it points to the central tendon, retrieve the septum transversum.

CVP-A20:1.title: Trace closure of the posterolateral canals
body: The septum transversum forms a partial partition. Early on, gaps remain posterolaterally beside the foregut, allowing communication between the future pleural and peritoneal spaces. The pleuroperitoneal folds grow to meet the septum transversum and the dorsal esophageal mesentery, then merge with the developing body-wall component. This establishes separation while leaving defined routes for vessels and esophagus.

Pleuroperitoneal and pleuropericardial membranes have different destinations. The first separate pleural spaces from the abdominal peritoneal cavity, while the latter separate pleural from pericardial spaces. Use the name to recall the two spaces involved. A defect of posterolateral closure permits abdominal viscera to enter the thorax, which can restrict development of lung tissue.
CVP-A20:1.example: On the paired textbook cross-sections, follow the fold closing the gap toward the esophageal mesentery. Do not misidentify the normal aortic route as the posterolateral defect.

CVP-A20:2.title: Explain cervical roots despite the adult position
body: Early diaphragmatic structures lie cranially in the embryo, near the cervical levels that supply the phrenic nerves. As the partition shifts caudally with growth, the phrenic nerves retain their cervical connection and run down through the thorax to reach the mature diaphragm. Thus the mature position of a muscle alone does not predict its nerve roots.

Phrenic nerves (C3–C5) provide the diaphragm’s motor supply. Sensation from central diaphragmatic pleura also travels by phrenic nerves, which explains shoulder referral. Peripheral diaphragmatic pleural sensation travels through lower intercostal nerves. Do not use the source slide’s peripheral body-wall wording to replace phrenic motor supply with intercostal innervation.
CVP-A20:2.example: Compare a question about contraction of a hemidiaphragm with one about localized pain from its peripheral pleural covering. The first asks for phrenic motor supply; the second asks for somatic sensory supply from intercostal nerves.

CVP-A20:resp26-contributions.title: Read the developmental cross-sections in sequence
body: Begin with the axial sketch before a complete diaphragm has formed. Orient by the posterior vertebral column, then locate the aorta, esophagus and inferior vena cava. As the septum transversum appears, it fills much of the anterior partition while posterior communications remain. Locate the dorsal mesentery around the esophagus before tracking the folds that close the posterolateral gaps.

In the later sketches, peripheral muscle extends in from the body wall, surrounding the more central contributions. The resulting openings relate to different parts of the partition rather than all lying in a single flat layer. Move between early and late drawings by following a fixed landmark such as the esophagus or posterior aorta. This makes the arrows in the four-component figure easier to interpret.

To interpret the sequence without color, use position and timing. The anterior plate appears while the posterolateral channels are still open. The folds extend into those channels from the posterolateral wall. Tissue around the esophagus sits closer to the midline and supplies the posterior crural contribution. A final section with a continuous perimeter and defined openings represents fusion and muscle ingrowth, not persistence of the original broad communication.
CVP-A20:resp26-contributions.example: If a late section labels the central tendon, identify the earlier component in the anterior partial partition. Then find the separate contribution around the esophagus.

CVP-A20:resp26-descent.title: Locate the caval, esophageal and aortic routes
body: Read T8, T10 and T12 from superior to inferior. The IVC crosses the central tendon at the caval opening near T8. The esophagus traverses a muscular hiatus formed mainly by fibers of the right crus near T10, accompanied by the vagal trunks. The aorta travels posterior to the diaphragm between the crura near T12, typically with the thoracic duct.

These levels distinguish passages through tendon, through muscle, and posterior to the diaphragm. They are not boundaries of the domes, which move with breathing. Posterior orientation matters: on an axial diagram, locate the vertebral column first, then the most posterior of the three routes.
The diaphragm retains phrenic innervation from C3–C5 after descent. Central pleural sensation travels in those nerves; peripheral diaphragmatic pleural sensation uses intercostal nerves.
CVP-A20:resp26-descent.example: A structure just anterior to the vertebral column passing behind the diaphragm belongs to the aortic route. A structure passing through the central tendon belongs to the caval route.

CVP-A20:resp26-hernia.title: Distinguish a closure defect from other diaphragm abnormalities
body: A Bochdalek-type congenital diaphragmatic hernia is posterolateral. The developmental defect can leave continuity between the abdominal and pleural spaces, allowing viscera to move into the thorax. This crowds the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia. The adverse effect is therefore present before birth and is more than temporary displacement of a fully formed lung.

A hiatal hernia instead uses the normal esophageal opening, and eventration describes an abnormally elevated but continuous diaphragm. Use both the location and the continuity of the partition to distinguish the mechanisms. The course emphasizes posterolateral fusion failure. Exact severity varies with how much lung growth was restricted.

After herniation, a question may distinguish a displaced mediastinum from true loss of developing lung tissue. Displacement describes what the neighboring organs do. Hypoplasia describes the reduced growth of the lung itself. The two can coexist. Even if the herniated bowel is repositioned, the amount of prenatal lung development already achieved remains relevant to how well the lung can function.
CVP-A20:resp26-hernia.example: Bowel in the thorax through a posterolateral gap plus a small ipsilateral lung points to a closure defect with hypoplasia. An intact elevated dome supports eventration instead.

The vagal trunks pass with the esophagus at the muscular hiatus near T10.

CVP-A21:0.title: Compare thoracic motor outputs by their routes
body: For a somatic motor example, trace a single motor neuron from the CNS to skeletal muscle. The diaphragm is an example via the phrenic nerve. For an autonomic motor example, trace two neurons: a preganglionic neuron in the CNS and a postganglionic neuron in a peripheral ganglion. Thoracic autonomic targets include myocardium, airway smooth muscle and glands.

A cardiac sympathetic axon starts in upper thoracic cord and enters the sympathetic chain; the postganglionic axon proceeds to the cardiac plexus. A vagal cardiac parasympathetic axon starts in the medulla and usually travels nearly all the way to the heart before synapsing. Identify the synapse before deciding whether a labeled fiber is preganglionic or postganglionic.
Cardiac sympathetic output increases heart rate and conduction, whereas parasympathetic output slows them. Signals returning from organs are visceral afferents.
CVP-A21:0.example: A nerve running in the thorax can contain visceral afferents or autonomic motor fibers, or can supply skeletal muscle. Determine the target and direction rather than classifying the nerve from location alone.

CVP-A21:1.title: Explain cardiac referred pain from shared spinal segments
body: Cardiac ischemia can activate visceral pain afferents. They often accompany sympathetic pathways on the way back toward upper thoracic spinal segments, but their cell bodies are in dorsal root ganglia. They pass through sympathetic ganglia without using those ganglia as a motor-style synapse.

Visceral input and somatic input converge onto overlapping second-order neurons in the spinal cord. The brain can localize cardiac input to a familiar somatic area, such as the chest or medial arm. This is a central interpretation of shared segmental input, rather than direct injury to the arm or the vagus carrying motor output to the skin.
CVP-A21:1.example: Compare chest and medial-arm referral with shoulder referral from central diaphragmatic pleura. Both rely on shared spinal processing, but the cardiac pattern is upper thoracic and the pleural pattern involves phrenic C3–C5 pathways.

CVP-A21:2.title: Use the vagus to distinguish reflex input and motor output
body: CN X contains multiple fiber types. Preganglionic parasympathetic efferents travel from medullary nuclei to ganglia near or within thoracic organs. Short postganglionic axons then act on targets. Visceral sensory fibers in the same nerve travel toward the brainstem and convey reflex information. Their presence does not change the definition of preganglionic motor fibers.

In the heart, vagal activity primarily slows the sinoatrial node and reduces atrioventricular conduction. In the lungs, parasympathetic output promotes airway smooth-muscle constriction and gland secretion. Afferent traffic contributes to regulatory reflexes, such as signals about lung stretch. Compare both routes with the phrenic nerve's somatic motor supply to diaphragm.
CVP-A21:2.example: A fiber carrying information about airway stretch toward the brainstem is an afferent. A fiber carrying a signal from the medulla to a ganglion in the airway is a preganglionic efferent.

CVP-A21:resp26-organization.title: Read neuron shape and functional direction
body: The CNS is brain and spinal cord; cranial nerves, spinal nerves and peripheral ganglia are PNS structures. Somatic motor pathways act on skeletal muscle. Autonomic motor pathways act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle and glands. Sensory traffic can serve either somatic or visceral functions, so motor division and sensory origin are separate classifications.

In the slide comparing neuron shapes, the pseudounipolar cell has one process dividing into central and peripheral branches. This is the usual sensory cell type in a dorsal root ganglion. Bipolar cells have two processes extending from opposite sides of the cell body, whereas multipolar cells have many dendrites and one axon, as with spinal somatic motor neurons. Dendrites are generally receptive; the axon is the conducting output process.
CVP-A21:resp26-organization.example: Locate a ganglion on the dorsal root in the course diagram. Then identify which neuron diagram can carry a peripheral signal to the CNS without a synapse in that ganglion.

CVP-A21:resp26-spinal.title: Trace roots, rami and sympathetic communications
body: Follow the diagram from the cord outwards. Dorsal roots carry sensory traffic and contain the dorsal root ganglion. Ventral roots carry efferent traffic. The two unite to form a mixed spinal nerve, which then divides into mixed dorsal and ventral rami. A posterior ramus serves posterior body territories, but it is mixed; do not assign it the purely sensory function of a dorsal root.

Preganglionic sympathetic somata lie in the intermediolateral cell column at T1–L2 in the course scheme. Their axons exit through ventral roots, enter the spinal nerve, then travel to the trunk through myelinated white rami. Unmyelinated postganglionic axons return through gray rami to spinal nerves at all levels, supplying structures such as cutaneous vessels and sweat glands. Organ-directed sympathetic branches can leave the chain directly instead.
CVP-A21:resp26-spinal.example: Use the numbered drawing to follow a somatic sensory fiber, a somatic motor fiber and a sympathetic fiber in different colors. Identify the first point where each route diverges from the others.

CVP-A21:resp26-sympathetic.title: Follow sympathetic fibers to heart and lungs
body: Trace the cardiac example from the upper thoracic intermediolateral region (T1–T4 in this lecture) through a ventral root and white ramus. A preganglionic axon can ascend the trunk before synapsing in a cervical ganglion, or synapse in an upper thoracic ganglion. The postganglionic fiber leaves toward the cardiac plexus; it need not return through a gray ramus to the spinal nerve.

Cardiac sympathetic output increases SA rate, AV conduction and myocardial contractility. Cardiopulmonary splanchnic branches are chiefly postganglionic. Contrast them with the greater and lesser thoracic splanchnic nerves to abdominal prevertebral ganglia, which principally carry preganglionic fibers. The diagrams put both near the same sympathetic chain; destination and synapse distinguish them.
CVP-A21:resp26-sympathetic.example: If a fiber has already synapsed in the cervical sympathetic trunk and is heading to the cardiac plexus, label it postganglionic. Do not infer fiber order from the word splanchnic alone.

CVP-A21:resp26-vagal.title: Locate the parasympathetic relay near the organ
body: In the vagal route, the long preganglionic axon leaves the medulla in CN X. It travels to terminal ganglia near or within the organ, where a short postganglionic neuron takes over. The lecture names the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus; cardiac parasympathetic neurons also arise importantly in the nucleus ambiguus, so the dorsal motor nucleus is not exclusive.

At the heart, prioritize SA and AV nodal effects: lower rate and slower conduction. Direct vagal influence on ventricular contractility is relatively limited. At the airway, vagal parasympathetic activity promotes constriction and secretion. Vascular caliber cannot be predicted reliably from a one-line sympathetic-versus-vagal rule because local metabolic and mechanical influences also matter.
CVP-A21:resp26-vagal.example: On the comparative route diagram, circle the sympathetic chain relay and the vagal terminal relay. Use their positions to compare the lengths of preganglionic and postganglionic axons.

CVP-A21:resp26-afferents.title: Distinguish pain, reflex and efferent pathways
body: Start with the question “Which direction is the signal going?” Sympathetic and parasympathetic efferents leave the CNS and synapse in their respective ganglia. Visceral afferents return information. A cardiac pain afferent can accompany a sympathetic bundle without being a sympathetic motor neuron. For spinal cardiac pain, its soma is in a dorsal root ganglion, and its central process enters through the dorsal root.

Vagal sensory afferents support physiological reflexes, carrying information such as stretch toward the brainstem. Contrast three roles in one scenario: visceral sensing triggers a reflex, CNS integration changes autonomic output, and motor neurons alter the target’s activity. This prevents confusion between a first-order sensory soma and a postganglionic motor soma.
CVP-A21:resp26-afferents.example: A drug changes cardiac vagal motor output but spares sensory afferents. Predict that a motor response can change even though the incoming visceral information remains available.
