CVP-A22:cardinal.title: Trace the cardinal routes into the adult SVC
body: Draw the right and left anterior cardinal veins draining the cranial embryo. Each joins its side's posterior cardinal vein to make a common cardinal vein entering the sinus venosus. A transverse anastomosis transfers flow from left to right. The anastomosis persists as the left brachiocephalic vein; the right anterior cardinal segment below it and the right common cardinal vein form the SVC.

Follow the fate of each segment rather than calling the entire embryonic right vein “the SVC.” The upper drainage pathways still exist on both sides. Persistence of the left-sided channel can produce a left SVC, commonly draining to the coronary sinus, sometimes with the right SVC still present.
CVP-A22:cardinal.example: On a bilateral diagram, color the transverse bridge first and the remaining right-sided vertical segment second. They have different adult names.

CVP-A22:ivc.title: Build the IVC from hepatic, renal and caudal segments
body: Read the IVC from liver downward. The hepatic segment uses the right vitelline-derived hepatocardiac channel. The prerenal segment chiefly uses the right subcardinal vein. The renal segment forms through anastomoses around the kidneys. The postrenal segment chiefly uses the right supracardinal vein. The IVC is assembled from several channels with different drainage territories.

The renal-level connections explain why knowing “right supracardinal” alone is inadequate. If an infrarenal channel persists on both sides, the result can be a duplicated IVC. If continuity toward the hepatic portion fails, azygos continuation can carry lower-body venous return toward the SVC.
CVP-A22:ivc.example: For an infrarenal abnormality, start with supracardinal persistence. For a hepatic-segment question, start with the vitelline-derived connection.

CVP-A22:fetal-veins.title: Distinguish cardinal, vitelline and umbilical return
body: Start by naming the tissue being drained. Cardinal veins drain the embryo itself. Vitelline veins drain the yolk sac and are remodeled around the gut and liver, contributing to the portal system and hepatic IVC connection. Umbilical veins return oxygenated blood from the placenta. These pathways converge centrally, but their origins and developmental fates are different.

The left umbilical vein persists during fetal life. Some of its flow enters the hepatic circulation, and some can reach the IVC through the ductus venosus. After birth, the left umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres of the liver, while the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
CVP-A22:fetal-veins.example: Distinguish a fetal route that bypasses part of the liver from the ductus arteriosus, which connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta.

CVP-A22:0.title: Use the drained territory to identify the embryonic vein
body: A vessel carrying placental blood belongs to the umbilical system; one collecting yolk-sac or early gut drainage belongs to the vitelline system; one returning blood from the embryo proper belongs to the cardinal system. This sorting remains useful before the adult liver and caval pathways take shape. Oxygen content alone is not a reliable definition of an artery or vein: the fetal umbilical vein carries relatively oxygen-rich blood toward the fetus.

CVP-A22:1.title: Read venous asymmetry as persistence plus regression
body: Adult venous drainage is asymmetric because some embryonic connections enlarge while others regress. On the superior diagram, left-sided cranial return crosses through the brachiocephalic bridge to the right SVC. The left-sided heartward segment usually regresses. A persistent left-sided channel can connect to the coronary sinus, which is why an enlarged coronary sinus can provide a clue. Apply this reasoning to the direction of drainage rather than expecting all adult right-sided vessels to arise from one embryonic vein.

CVP-A22:2.title: Follow placental flow before and after birth
body: In fetal life, trace placenta → left umbilical vein → liver or ductus venosus → IVC → right atrium. At birth, placental flow stops, and these fetal hepatic channels no longer serve their prenatal roles. The portal system continues to carry blood from the gut to the liver. A change in placental flow is therefore different from closure or obstruction of adult portal drainage.

CVP-A23:heart-review.title: Locate a cardiac developmental defect by its pathway
body: Orient the early cardiac tube by inflow and outflow before interpreting a malformation. Venous inflow enters the caudal end, while blood exits cranially. Looping changes the spatial relationships of the future chambers without immediately producing complete septation. A defect of looping changes position; a defect of septation can leave abnormal communication even when gross orientation is otherwise normal.

For an integrated question, ask whether the problem is a misplaced chamber, a persistent intracardiac opening, or a great-vessel connection. Predict blood flow only after tracing the actual opening and comparing pressures. An embryonic communication can be normal in fetal life and abnormal if it persists beyond its expected closure.

When a question describes a change after birth, distinguish anatomy from pressure-driven flow. The fetal foramen ovale permits right-to-left flow when right atrial pressure is higher. After birth, increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure and can press the flap closed. That functional closure comes before any anatomical fusion. A flap mechanism, a missing septal tissue segment, and a persistent extracardiac channel are different findings even if each can affect blood mixing.

CVP-A23:lung-review.title: Separate three mechanisms of developmental respiratory distress
body: Use the location of the developmental error. Abnormal foregut separation can create a tracheoesophageal connection. Immature distal gas-exchange units and insufficient surfactant reduce stability during breathing. A posterolateral diaphragm defect can allow viscera to restrict lung growth. These mechanisms can all present as respiratory distress but have different structural evidence.
CVP-A23:lung-review.example: Coughing with feeds and an abnormal lumen favor a foregut communication. Small lungs next to herniated bowel favor hypoplasia. A premature infant with poor alveolar inflation can have surfactant-related disease without either structural connection.

CVP-A23:0.title: Work backward from the defect to the embryonic step
body: Name the two structures that should be separated before naming the partition. Ventral airway versus dorsal esophagus implicates tracheoesophageal partitioning. Pleural versus pericardial cavity implicates pleuropericardial membranes. Pleural versus peritoneal cavity implicates pleuroperitoneal closure. The terms look alike, but the two compartments reveal the answer.

CVP-A23:1.title: Predict what can flow through an abnormal connection
body: Air can pass from a distal tracheal connection into the stomach if the distal esophagus remains open to it. Swallowed material cannot pass normally through a proximal blind pouch. In a diaphragm defect, the abnormal route permits movement of organs between cavities rather than communication between two epithelial tubes. Identify what is able to cross before explaining the symptoms.

CVP-A23:2.title: Compare tissue formation with postnatal function
body: The presence of a lung bud proves initiation but does not show adequate branching, vascular development, surface area or surfactant. Compare a loss of lung volume after compression with a biochemical failure of alveolar stability. Oxygenation ultimately depends on both adequate perfusion and ventilation at thin, functioning distal exchange surfaces.

CVP-P15:hemodynamic-case.title: Read cardiovascular cases as a pressure–flow chain
body: Start with mean arterial pressure as cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance, with right atrial pressure subtracted from arterial pressure in the full relation. Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume. Stroke volume in turn depends on filling, afterload and contractility. Tracing the chain prevents interpreting a low blood pressure as proof of low resistance or low cardiac output without further evidence.
CVP-P15:hemodynamic-case.example: If stroke volume falls from 70 to 45 mL at 80 beats/min, cardiac output falls from 5.6 to 3.6 L/min. A rise in resistance can partially maintain pressure even though flow is lower. Predict how compensatory tachycardia and venoconstriction might modify that picture.

CVP-P15:operating-point.title: Read the intersection of cardiac and venous-return curves
body: At steady state, cardiac output equals venous return. Plot both against right atrial pressure. Increased contractility raises the cardiac function curve; it can increase flow at a lower right atrial pressure. Increased stressed blood volume raises mean systemic filling pressure, shifting venous return toward greater flow at a given right atrial pressure.

A change in resistance to venous return alters slope. An increase in mean systemic filling pressure moves the zero-flow intercept. Identify the axis and intercept before saying that a curve shifted. If both curves move, their new intersection determines the combined result.

Use the venous-return equation as a check: flow = (mean systemic filling pressure − right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return. With filling pressure 7 mmHg, right atrial pressure 2 mmHg and resistance 1 mmHg·min/L, return is 5 L/min. Raising the filling pressure to 9 mmHg raises return to 7 L/min at that same right atrial pressure; the actual steady-state operating point also depends on the cardiac curve. A measured rise in right atrial pressure can oppose part of the initial gain in return.

CVP-P15:0.title: Compare compensation with the original disturbance
body: With acute blood loss, the initiating change is a fall in circulating volume and venous return. Reduced ventricular filling lowers stroke volume. Reflex sympathetic activation can raise heart rate, contractility, venous tone and arteriolar resistance. Those responses are compensations and may not completely restore output. A patient can therefore show tachycardia and cold extremities while still having low flow.

CVP-P15:1.title: Distinguish resistance, pressure difference and flow
body: Use flow = pressure difference divided by resistance. Greater pressure upstream does not guarantee greater flow if resistance also rises. If the same 90 mmHg pressure difference acts across twice the resistance, flow is halved. In a regional vascular bed this predicts reduced flow even when systemic pressure is maintained. Specify the pressure difference across the bed rather than quoting only the upstream pressure.

CVP-P15:2.title: Choose the observation that would distinguish mechanisms
body: A decrease in arterial pressure could result from low cardiac output, vasodilation or both. Use additional information such as heart rate, ventricular filling and whether extremities are warm or cool to test competing explanations. Individual signs are context dependent. A good exam explanation names the initiating change, the first measurable consequence, and the compensatory change separately.

CVP-P26:oxygen-levels.title: Separate arterial oxygen tension, content and delivery
body: Hypoxemia refers to low arterial oxygen tension. Tissue hypoxia can result from poor oxygen delivery or impaired cellular oxygen use even with a normal PaO₂. Oxygen content depends mainly on hemoglobin amount and saturation; dissolved oxygen contributes much less. Delivery also depends on blood flow, so PaO₂ alone cannot distinguish all causes of impaired tissue oxygenation.
CVP-P26:oxygen-levels.example: At the same PaO₂ and saturation, halving hemoglobin roughly halves the hemoglobin-bound component. Normal arterial oxygen tension therefore does not rule out low oxygen delivery in severe anemia.

CVP-P26:gradient.title: Calculate and interpret the alveolar–arterial difference
body: Estimate alveolar oxygen tension with PAO₂ ≈ FIO₂ × (barometric pressure − water vapor pressure) − PaCO₂/R. The A–a difference is PAO₂ minus measured arterial PaO₂. State the assumptions, especially inspired oxygen and barometric pressure. At sea level on room air, using 760 mmHg, 47 mmHg and R = 0.8 with PaCO₂ 40 mmHg gives PAO₂ near 100 mmHg.
CVP-P26:gradient.example: With PaO₂ 60 mmHg under those assumptions, the difference is about 40 mmHg. Low arterial and alveolar oxygen together with a relatively preserved difference suggests low inspired oxygen or hypoventilation; a widened difference supports V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation or shunt.

CVP-P26:oxygen-response.title: Use the oxygen response to compare gas-exchange defects
body: Low V/Q units receive some ventilation, so supplemental oxygen can improve their end-capillary oxygenation. Diffusion limitation can also improve with a larger oxygen gradient. A true right-to-left shunt sends some blood past ventilated alveoli, so that fraction cannot equilibrate with the higher inspired oxygen. Large shunts therefore respond less completely.
The response is a clue, not a standalone diagnosis. Multiple mechanisms may coexist. Use the A–a difference and clinical context before deciding which mechanism dominates.

CVP-P26:0.title: Work through four ways tissue oxygen delivery can fail
body: Low arterial oxygen tension, low hemoglobin, low flow and inability to use delivered oxygen are different failures. The first is hypoxemia; the second lowers blood content; the third lowers delivery even when content is adequate; the fourth impairs extraction or utilization. In a flow-limited region, increasing PaO₂ may raise dissolved oxygen but does not correct the original perfusion defect.

CVP-P26:1.title: Distinguish reduced alveolar oxygen from failed transfer
body: If hypoventilation raises PaCO₂, the alveolar gas equation predicts a lower PAO₂. Arterial oxygen can then fall while the A–a difference remains comparatively preserved. If alveolar oxygen remains adequate but PaO₂ is low, the larger difference directs attention to transfer or mixing. Always calculate PAO₂ under the actual gas and altitude assumptions rather than subtracting from a fixed 100 mmHg.

CVP-P26:2.title: Use exercise to reason about diffusion reserve
body: Exercise raises flow and can shorten pulmonary capillary transit time. Healthy lungs usually have enough reserve for oxygen equilibration; a thickened barrier or reduced effective surface can expose limited reserve during exertion. That pattern differs from a completely unventilated but perfused unit, where there is no fresh alveolar oxygen supply to that blood even at rest.

CVP-P27:gravity.title: Distinguish regional amounts from regional V/Q ratios
body: In an upright lung, ventilation and perfusion generally both increase toward the base, but perfusion changes more. The ratio is therefore higher at the apex and lower at the base. A high apical V/Q does not mean the apex receives the greatest absolute ventilation; it means ventilation is high relative to its blood flow.

As V/Q rises, alveolar gas approaches inspired gas with relatively higher oxygen and lower CO₂. As V/Q falls, alveolar gas approaches mixed venous values. Always compare ventilation and perfusion together before predicting the gas composition.

Compare two simplified units. One receives 0.5 units of ventilation and 0.25 of perfusion, giving V/Q = 2. Another receives 1.5 ventilation and 2.5 perfusion, giving V/Q = 0.6. The second receives more absolute ventilation but has the lower ratio. The blood leaving it also contributes more to the mixed arterial sample. That is why interpreting a whole-lung number requires both regional ratios and their blood-flow weighting.

CVP-P27:extremes.title: Use zero and infinity to identify the limiting cases
body: An airway obstruction with preserved blood flow approaches V/Q = 0, the shunt limit. A perfusion obstruction with continued ventilation approaches V/Q → infinity, the alveolar dead-space limit. Both create inefficiency, but one returns poorly oxygenated blood and the other wastes ventilation.
CVP-P27:extremes.example: If ventilation is 2 units and perfusion is 0, the ratio has no finite value and the ventilated unit contributes no gas transfer to blood. If ventilation is 0 and perfusion is 2, the blood leaves without exposure to fresh alveolar gas.

CVP-P27:0.title: Predict end-capillary gas in a low V/Q unit
body: When ventilation falls relative to perfusion, fresh oxygen is delivered more slowly and CO₂ is removed less efficiently per unit of flow. End-capillary blood leaving that unit tends to have lower oxygen and higher CO₂ than blood from a better-matched unit. Partial ventilation distinguishes low V/Q from a true shunt; a rise in inspired oxygen can still reach a partially ventilated unit.

CVP-P27:1.title: Explain why dead-space ventilation raises the work of breathing
body: A perfusion defect leaves some alveoli ventilated without useful exchange. For the same minute ventilation, a smaller fraction reaches perfused exchange units. Maintaining effective ventilation can then require a higher minute ventilation. Contrast this with shunt, where blood continues to flow through an unventilated region and mixes with blood from other areas.

CVP-P27:2.title: Explain why high V/Q regions cannot fully compensate for low ones
body: Hemoglobin in well-ventilated units is already near the plateau of the oxygen dissociation curve. Further raising their alveolar oxygen adds comparatively little oxygen content. When poorly oxygenated blood mixes with that blood, the deficit can persist. Judge the mixture by blood oxygen content and the fraction of flow from each region, not by averaging regional oxygen tensions.

CVP-P28:control.title: Trace the ventilation feedback loop
body: Separate sensor, integrator, motor output and response. Chemoreceptors respond to chemical changes, brainstem networks integrate the signals, and respiratory motor neurons alter inspiratory and expiratory muscle activity. If arterial CO₂ rises because ventilation fell, increased respiratory drive raises alveolar ventilation and helps bring CO₂ back down. That opposing effect makes the loop negative feedback.
CVP-P28:control.example: An increase in total breathing does not guarantee the same increase in alveolar ventilation. If breaths are shallow, a greater fraction of each breath may ventilate dead space.

CVP-P28:chemoreceptors.title: Compare central and peripheral chemoreceptor signals
body: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier and changes hydrogen ion concentration in brain extracellular fluid and CSF. Central chemoreception therefore tracks the effect of CO₂ on local pH. Peripheral chemoreceptors, especially carotid bodies, rapidly respond to low arterial PaO₂ and also respond to changes in arterial CO₂ and pH.

Separate a fall in oxygen tension from a fall in oxygen content. Carotid-body stimulation by hypoxemia concerns PaO₂; anemia can reduce content without lowering PaO₂ to the same degree. Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to a metabolic acid load even when CO₂ is not the primary disturbance.

CVP-P28:reflexes.title: Compare stretch, irritant and pulmonary congestion signals
body: Lung mechanoreceptors and airway sensory endings provide feedback through vagal afferents. Large lung inflation activates slowly adapting stretch receptors, which can inhibit inspiration. Airway irritation can trigger protective responses such as cough. Sensory endings associated with pulmonary congestion can contribute to rapid shallow breathing. These signals are distinct from arterial blood chemistry.
CVP-P28:reflexes.example: Ask whether the first change is lung inflation, an airway irritant, or a fall in arterial oxygen tension. That identifies the sensor category before you predict the breathing response.

CVP-P28:0.title: Predict the central response to acute CO₂ retention
body: When PaCO₂ rises, CO₂ diffuses into the brain and generates hydrogen ions. A fall in local pH increases ventilatory drive. Over time, buffering and bicarbonate adjustment modify the sustained stimulus, so acute and chronic changes need not have the same effect. Arterial hydrogen ions themselves do not cross as freely as CO₂.

CVP-P28:1.title: Identify the signal during acute ascent
body: At altitude, lower barometric pressure reduces inspired oxygen partial pressure even though the fraction of oxygen is still about 21%. The fall in PaO₂ stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors and promotes hyperventilation. The resulting fall in PaCO₂ raises pH and can oppose part of the drive centrally. Separate the initiating hypoxic stimulus from the downstream CO₂ change.

CVP-P28:2.title: Predict the direction of compensation for metabolic acidosis
body: When arterial pH falls because of a metabolic acid load, peripheral chemoreceptors help drive increased ventilation. Lower PaCO₂ reduces the respiratory contribution to acidity. This is compensation for the primary metabolic disturbance. In a case, name the primary change first, then show how the ventilatory response pushes pH in the opposite direction.

summary: Glycogenin primes the chain; glycogen synthase uses UDP-glucose to extend α(1→4) bonds and branching enzyme makes α(1→6) bonds.
Phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate at nonreducing ends; debranching glucosidase releases free glucose from α(1→6) junctions.
Insulin favors storage; hepatic glucagon/cAMP/PKA favors mobilization. Skeletal muscle uses contraction-related signals and epinephrine.
Liver releases glucose using glucose-6-phosphatase; muscle lacks that enzyme and uses glycogen locally. Distinguish Pompe, McArdle and Von Gierke by the blocked step.

MOL-20:synthesis.title: Build glycogen from activated glucose and then branch it
body: Trace glucose-6-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate through phosphoglucomutase, then to UDP-glucose through UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase. UDP-glucose is the activated donor. Glycogenin supplies a primer, and glycogen synthase extends existing nonreducing ends by making α(1→4) bonds. A branching enzyme moves a short terminal chain to form an α(1→6) linkage, creating another nonreducing end.

Branching increases solubility and the number of sites at which enzymes can add or remove residues at the same time. The chain elongation and branch-forming reactions therefore solve different problems. A defect in branching can leave long, poorly soluble chains even though synthase still extends them.

MOL-20:mobilization.title: Trace glycogen breakdown past a branch point
body: Glycogen phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate to cleave α(1→4) bonds from nonreducing ends, yielding glucose-1-phosphate. It stops near an α(1→6) branch. A transferase moves three residues to a neighboring chain, exposing the last α(1→6)-linked glucose. Debranching glucosidase hydrolyzes that bond to release free glucose. Phosphorylase can then resume.
MOL-20:mobilization.example: Most residues emerge as glucose-1-phosphate, while the branch-point residue emerges as free glucose. Distinguish phosphorolysis from hydrolysis before identifying the product.

MOL-20:regulation.title: Predict how fed and fasting signals change glycogen flux
body: In the fed state, insulin promotes storage, including dephosphorylation that favors glycogen synthase activity and lowers phosphorylase activity. During fasting, glucagon in liver drives cAMP and protein kinase A signaling, activating the phosphorylase cascade and opposing glycogen synthesis. Skeletal muscle responds to epinephrine and contraction-related signals such as Ca²⁺ and AMP, rather than using glucagon as the main glycogenolytic signal.
MOL-20:regulation.example: A phosphorylation switch can activate one enzyme and inhibit another. Ask whether the target is glycogen synthase or phosphorylase before predicting the direction.

MOL-20:disease.title: Locate an enzyme defect from tissue and timing
body: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency blocks the last step for hepatic glucose release, so both glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis are impaired at their common endpoint. Muscle phosphorylase deficiency limits use of muscle glycogen during intense exercise and is associated with exercise intolerance. A lysosomal acid α-glucosidase defect instead affects lysosomal glycogen degradation, distinct from cytosolic phosphorylase.
MOL-20:disease.example: Start with fasting hypoglycemia versus exercise symptoms versus lysosomal storage. Then identify the affected compartment and enzyme instead of using glycogen accumulation alone.

MOL-20:0.title: Identify the reducing end and the sites of rapid turnover
body: A glycogen molecule is organized around a single reducing end associated with glycogenin and many nonreducing ends. Branch points use α(1→6) linkages and chain segments use α(1→4). Increasing branches increases the number of places where synthesis and breakdown can run in parallel. On a diagram, identify chain tips separately from branch junctions.

MOL-20:1.title: Compare products at a straight chain and a branch
body: On a straight chain, phosphorylase uses phosphate to release glucose-1-phosphate, preserving an already phosphorylated intermediate. At an α(1→6) junction, a hydrolase uses water to release free glucose. If a question specifies a branch residue, its product differs from most glucose residues in the same molecule.

MOL-20:2.title: Trace why liver and muscle glycogen serve different goals
body: Both tissues can convert glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate. Liver can remove the phosphate and release free glucose to the circulation. Skeletal muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and sends the carbon into its own glycolysis. The key distinction is what happens after mobilization; muscle can break down glycogen efficiently even though it cannot export its phosphorylated product as blood glucose.

summary: The oxidative PPP yields ribulose-5-phosphate, CO₂ and two NADPH per glucose-6-phosphate; ATP is not a direct output.
The reversible nonoxidative phase reshuffles carbon: transketolase moves two carbons using TPP, and transaldolase moves three.
Match pathway direction to NADPH versus ribose demand. Erythrocytes need NADPH to regenerate GSH; G6PD deficiency predisposes to oxidant-induced hemolysis.

MOL-21:oxidative.title: Account for carbon and NADPH in the oxidative PPP
body: Glucose-6-phosphate enters the irreversible oxidative phase through G6PD. A second oxidative step later produces another NADPH and releases CO₂ as the six-carbon intermediate becomes ribulose-5-phosphate. Per glucose-6-phosphate, the standard outputs are two NADPH, one CO₂ and one five-carbon sugar phosphate. ATP is not a direct product of these oxidative reactions.

NADPH provides reducing power for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense. The pentose can become ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides or enter reversible carbon rearrangements. Track the lost carbon separately from the source of reducing equivalents.

MOL-21:rearrangement.title: Match reversible carbon rearrangements to demand
body: Transketolase transfers two-carbon units and requires thiamine pyrophosphate; transaldolase transfers three-carbon units. These reactions interconvert pentose phosphates with fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Unlike the oxidative phase, the rearrangements themselves do not make NADPH or release CO₂.

If nucleotide synthesis needs ribose more than NADPH, the cell can use glycolytic intermediates in the reverse direction. If NADPH demand is high, the pentoses can be sent back toward glycolytic intermediates while the oxidative steps continue. Decide which output is required before selecting the pathway direction.

MOL-21:red-cells.title: Trace how low NADPH makes red cells vulnerable
body: Mature red cells depend heavily on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH. Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione, which glutathione peroxidase uses to detoxify peroxides. A G6PD defect limits the first step, so oxidant stress can damage hemoglobin and membrane proteins and precipitate hemolysis.
MOL-21:red-cells.example: Oxidized hemoglobin can form Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of those inclusions can leave bite cells. Trace the sequence NADPH shortage → less reduced glutathione → oxidative injury, rather than treating the inclusions as the enzyme defect.

MOL-21:0.title: Distinguish NADPH production from ribose production
body: NADPH is an electron carrier, while ribose-5-phosphate supplies carbon for nucleotide synthesis. The oxidative phase can provide both kinds of output, but a cell can also make ribose through reversible rearrangements without generating oxidative-phase NADPH. State whether the question asks for an oxidative product, an eventual pentose product, or a nonoxidative product.

MOL-21:1.title: Explain why an oxidant exposure triggers hemolysis
body: An oxidant challenge increases the rate at which reduced glutathione is consumed. A red cell with low G6PD activity struggles to replenish it because NADPH generation is limited. Baseline function can be adequate until demand exceeds reserve. This is an antioxidant failure, distinct from a failure to generate ATP by glycolysis.

MOL-21:2.title: Follow a two-carbon transfer without changing redox state
body: When transketolase moves two carbons from a donor to an acceptor, the donor gets two carbons shorter and the acceptor two longer. Total carbon is conserved, and there is no oxidative CO₂ loss. This lets the cell reshuffle carbon between sugar pools as demands shift. Recognize a two-carbon transfer before retrieving its TPP requirement.

summary: Superoxide dismutase generates hydrogen peroxide; H₂O₂ is not a radical but can form hydroxyl radicals in the presence of reduced iron.
Catalase and glutathione peroxidase remove peroxide. Peroxidase consumes GSH; glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate it.
Phagocyte NADPH oxidase produces superoxide during the respiratory burst; myeloperoxidase forms hypochlorous acid downstream. Contrast deficient oxidant production with impaired antioxidant defense.

MOL-22:formation.title: Follow superoxide through peroxide to radical formation
body: Single-electron reduction of oxygen can form superoxide. Superoxide dismutase converts it to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species without an unpaired electron; it can cross or act across compartments more readily than some radicals. In the presence of reduced iron, peroxide can generate highly reactive hydroxyl radicals through Fenton chemistry.

The sequence explains why converting superoxide is only a first defense. Peroxide must also be removed before it damages local lipids, proteins or DNA. Compare the identity of the oxidant with the enzyme that handles it.

Possible sources include electron leak from mitochondrial respiratory complexes and regulated production by NADPH oxidase. Nitric oxide synthase makes nitric oxide from arginine. Nitric oxide is a physiological signal, but it can also react with superoxide to form peroxynitrite. In a source question, distinguish a respiratory-chain by-product, an intentional phagocyte burst, and an enzyme-derived vascular signal.

MOL-22:defense.title: Trace the glutathione cycle and its energy source
body: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione (GSH) to reduce peroxide, leaving oxidized glutathione (GSSG). Glutathione reductase then uses NADPH to regenerate GSH. Catalase can also remove hydrogen peroxide, producing water and oxygen without drawing directly on the GSH cycle. The enzymes solve complementary parts of the defense system.
MOL-22:defense.example: If glutathione peroxidase works but NADPH is scarce, detoxification can initially consume GSH faster than it is regenerated. The limiting problem is recycling, not a failure to recognize peroxide.

MOL-22:injury.title: Contrast oxidative damage with a missing respiratory burst
body: Uncontrolled reactive species damage membranes and other cellular components. In contrast, phagocytes deliberately use NADPH oxidase to generate superoxide during the respiratory burst. Subsequent chemistry supports microbial killing. A defect of NADPH oxidase impairs this deliberate antimicrobial production, while G6PD deficiency impairs the ability of vulnerable cells to defend against oxidants.

In a phagocyte, myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to form hypochlorous acid. If NADPH oxidase fails, production is impaired upstream at superoxide; if myeloperoxidase fails, the upstream burst can still generate superoxide and peroxide. This distinction helps interpret a question that names one particular oxidant as the missing product.
MOL-22:injury.example: A neutrophil killing defect and an oxidant-induced red-cell injury can both involve NADPH-related pathways but act on opposite sides of the production-versus-defense balance.

MOL-22:0.title: Classify a reactive species by its chemistry
body: Superoxide and hydroxyl radicals have unpaired electrons. Hydrogen peroxide is reactive without being a radical. That difference matters because a nonradical intermediate can still give rise to a damaging radical near a transition metal. Do not use “oxidant” and “free radical” as synonyms.

MOL-22:1.title: Choose the enzyme from the substrate and product
body: Superoxide dismutase acts on superoxide, whereas catalase and glutathione peroxidase remove peroxide. Glutathione reductase acts on oxidized glutathione rather than peroxide. In a reaction diagram, identify whether the substrate is an oxygen species or a glutathione disulfide before choosing the enzyme.

MOL-22:2.title: Separate direct detoxification from recycling
body: Peroxidase removes a peroxide molecule while consuming reducing equivalents held in GSH. Reductase replenishes GSH using NADPH. As oxidative stress continues, both steps are required to maintain defense. A defect in reductase can therefore reduce peroxide clearance indirectly even if peroxidase is present.

summary: Fructokinase makes fructose-1-phosphate; aldolase B cleaves it. Fructokinase deficiency causes essential fructosuria, while aldolase B deficiency causes phosphate trapping and hypoglycemia.
Galactokinase deficiency favors galactitol accumulation and cataracts; GALT deficiency causes galactose-1-phosphate accumulation and systemic illness.
Lactase deficiency causes luminal osmotic retention and fermentation. Mannose enters glycolysis as fructose-6-phosphate. Aldose reductase uses NADPH; sorbitol dehydrogenase uses NAD⁺.

MOL-23:fructose.title: Distinguish benign fructosuria from phosphate trapping
body: In liver, fructokinase converts fructose to fructose-1-phosphate. Aldolase B cleaves it to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde, which feed central metabolism. Fructokinase deficiency blocks the first step and can cause benign essential fructosuria. Aldolase B deficiency lets fructose-1-phosphate accumulate after fructose exposure, trapping phosphate and lowering ATP.

Phosphate trapping impairs hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, explaining hypoglycemia after exposure. Trace the blocked substrate before interpreting the symptoms; the two enzyme defects interrupt the same route at different positions.

MOL-23:galactose.title: Distinguish galactokinase deficiency from classic galactosemia
body: Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose to galactose-1-phosphate. GALT transfers the uridyl group in the pathway converting galactose-1-phosphate into intermediates of glucose metabolism. In classic GALT deficiency, galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and systemic illness can develop after milk feeding. In galactokinase deficiency, unphosphorylated galactose can be converted to galactitol, with cataracts a prominent feature.
MOL-23:galactose.example: Both defects can involve galactitol formation. Systemic hepatic disease plus galactose-1-phosphate accumulation points to GALT rather than to an isolated inability to phosphorylate galactose.

MOL-23:other-sugars.title: Connect lactose digestion, mannose entry and sugar alcohols
body: Lactase at the intestinal brush border splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Loss of intestinal lactase leaves sugar in the lumen, leading to osmotic water retention and fermentation. This is distinct from a hepatic enzyme defect after galactose has already been absorbed. Mannose can be phosphorylated and converted to fructose-6-phosphate to enter glycolysis.

Aldose reductase consumes NADPH to reduce glucose to sorbitol. Sorbitol dehydrogenase converts it onward to fructose where that enzyme is active. Tissues that accumulate sorbitol can experience osmotic stress.

In the classic polyol sequence, an excess of intracellular glucose can supply substrate for aldose reductase. In the lens, relative limits on downstream metabolism favor osmotic accumulation of polyols. In galactose disorders, the corresponding sugar alcohol is galactitol, not sorbitol. Identify the parent sugar first: glucose gives sorbitol; galactose gives galactitol.

MOL-23:0.title: Use the accumulated intermediate to infer the fructose defect
body: High fructose-1-phosphate implies fructokinase acted, so the likely defect lies downstream at aldolase B. A block of fructokinase instead reduces formation of fructose-1-phosphate. Interpret a phosphorylated accumulated substrate as evidence that the preceding phosphorylation step is intact.

MOL-23:1.title: Separate a digestion problem from intracellular galactose handling
body: Unabsorbed lactose causes intestinal symptoms through luminal osmosis and bacterial fermentation. Absorbed galactose can still cause toxicity if its hepatic processing is defective. A question about symptoms after milk therefore needs another clue, such as whether the dominant finding is bloating and diarrhea, cataracts, or neonatal systemic illness.

MOL-23:2.title: Track reducing equivalents through the polyol pathway
body: The glucose-to-sorbitol step consumes NADPH. The sorbitol-to-fructose step uses NAD⁺ and forms NADH. These are distinct cofactors. If the second step is limited, sorbitol can accumulate while the first step still draws on NADPH. Ask which reaction is active before predicting the cofactor change.

summary: ADH oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde in the cytosol; ALDH oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetate, principally in mitochondria. Both generate NADH.
High NADH favors pyruvate-to-lactate and oxaloacetate-to-malate shifts, limiting gluconeogenesis, and contributes to lipid accumulation.
CYP2E1 is an inducible microsomal pathway using oxygen and NADPH that can generate ROS. Distinguish each enzyme, cofactor and accumulating substrate.

MOL-24:oxidation.title: Account for ethanol carbon and NADH in two compartments
body: Cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde and reduces NAD⁺ to NADH. Mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetate and produces another NADH. The carbon skeleton remains two-carbon through these two oxidations. Acetate can be activated to acetyl-CoA in tissues.
The high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio alters other reversible reactions even after identifying acetate as the carbon product. Keep the fate of carbon separate from the burden of reducing equivalents.

Aldehyde dehydrogenase removes the toxic intermediate, so acetaldehyde can accumulate if that step is impaired or inhibited even though the initial oxidation continues. ADH and ALDH both consume NAD⁺, which is why the cellular redox consequences cannot be explained by the acetate product alone. In a compartment question, associate cytosolic NADH with the initial ADH reaction and mitochondrial NADH with the major ALDH reaction.

MOL-24:redox.title: Predict which reactions shift with excess hepatic NADH
body: Excess NADH pushes pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate. This reduces substrates available for gluconeogenesis, helping explain fasting hypoglycemia after ethanol intake. More lactate can also accumulate. A high reducing state favors glycerol-3-phosphate formation and can inhibit fatty-acid oxidation, contributing to triacylglycerol accumulation.

Compare a fed person with a person who has already depleted much of their hepatic glycogen. The latter relies more heavily on gluconeogenesis. When excess NADH pushes pyruvate toward lactate, the loss of accessible gluconeogenic carbon is therefore more consequential for blood glucose. The same biochemical shift can produce different severity depending on prior nutritional state.
MOL-24:redox.example: For a fasting case, ask whether the liver can use lactate and other precursors to make glucose. Extra acetate supplies acetyl-CoA but does not provide net glucose carbon in humans.

MOL-24:0.title: Separate the role of ADH from the role of ALDH
body: Alcohol dehydrogenase makes the reactive acetaldehyde intermediate. Aldehyde dehydrogenase removes it by oxidizing it to acetate. Slower aldehyde oxidation raises acetaldehyde despite continued ethanol conversion. Identify which substrate accumulates before deciding which enzyme is impaired.

MOL-24:1.title: Explain lactate accumulation from redox rather than oxygen supply alone
body: Lactate dehydrogenase interconverts lactate and pyruvate according to substrate and redox availability. Increased NADH favors reduction of pyruvate, regenerating NAD⁺ while raising lactate. A high lactate therefore does not by itself establish a tissue oxygen-delivery failure. In this case, the clue is the redox shift from ethanol oxidation.

MOL-24:2.title: Distinguish the inducible microsomal route
body: CYP2E1 can oxidize ethanol in the microsomal system and is induced with chronic exposure. It uses oxygen and NADPH and can contribute to reactive oxygen species and drug interactions. This contrasts with the NAD⁺-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase route. Do not assign NADH production directly to every route that oxidizes ethanol.

A competing alcohol can occupy alcohol dehydrogenase and change the rate at which another alcohol is converted to toxic metabolites. The underlying principle is competition at the enzyme and slower production of downstream metabolites, not direct neutralization of those metabolites. Treat the booklet example as enzyme kinetics rather than a dosing or treatment instruction.

summary: B₁ supplies TPP for oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase; B₂ supplies FMN/FAD; B₃ supplies NAD⁺/NADP⁺; B₅ is part of CoA.
B₆ supplies PLP for amino-acid reactions, biotin transfers activated CO₂, and folate transfers one-carbon units. B₁₂ supports methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Folate and B₁₂ deficiencies overlap in impaired DNA synthesis; elevated methylmalonic acid favors B₁₂ dysfunction. Vitamin C supports iron-dependent collagen hydroxylation.

MOL-25:energy-vitamins.title: Match energy cofactors to the reaction they enable
body: Thiamine pyrophosphate supports oxidative decarboxylation of α-ketoacids and two-carbon transfer by transketolase. Riboflavin supplies FMN and FAD for oxidation–reduction reactions, including steps where flavins remain closely bound to enzymes. Niacin supplies NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, which transfer reducing equivalents in different cellular roles. Pantothenate is part of coenzyme A for acyl transfer.

Associate thiamine deficiency with impaired oxidative decarboxylation and characteristic neurologic or cardiovascular syndromes; niacin deficiency with pellagra, classically dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia; and riboflavin deficiency with mucocutaneous findings such as angular cheilitis. Findings can overlap, so a cofactor clue is often more discriminating than a single symptom.
MOL-25:energy-vitamins.example: A question asking about pyruvate dehydrogenase can name several cofactors. If it asks specifically about the initial decarboxylation of pyruvate, select TPP rather than a later electron-transfer cofactor.

MOL-25:amino-and-one-carbon.title: Separate PLP, biotin, folate and B₁₂ by their chemistry
body: PLP, derived from vitamin B₆, stabilizes intermediates in amino-acid reactions such as transamination and decarboxylation. Biotin carries activated CO₂ in carboxylases. Folate transfers one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis. B₁₂ participates in methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which are chemically different from PLP transamination or biotin-dependent carboxylation.

Both folate and B₁₂ deficiency can impair DNA synthesis. Elevated methylmalonic acid and neurologic manifestations favor B₁₂ deficiency. Homocysteine may rise in either deficiency, so it is less specific alone.

When a question distinguishes vitamin requirements during development, folate supports nucleotide synthesis and adequate intake around conception reduces the risk of neural tube defects. When it describes paresthesia and megaloblastic anemia, consider B₁₂ and test the methylmalonyl-CoA route separately. B₆-dependent transamination and biotin-dependent CO₂ transfer do not explain either combined pattern.

MOL-25:vitamin-c.title: Connect collagen hydroxylation to tissue fragility
body: Vitamin C helps maintain iron in the reduced state required by collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Hydroxylation supports stable collagen structure. Deficiency can therefore produce fragile capillaries, gum bleeding and poor wound healing. This is a connective-tissue mechanism rather than failure to activate a coagulation protein.
MOL-25:vitamin-c.example: Compare bleeding caused by fragile vessels with bleeding caused by impaired vitamin K-dependent clotting factor function. The shared symptom does not identify the same biochemical step.

MOL-25:0.title: Use a reaction clue to recognize thiamine dependence
body: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate and branched-chain α-ketoacids shares a TPP-dependent early step. Transketolase also uses TPP but transfers carbon without decarboxylating an α-ketoacid. Recognize TPP from the reaction mechanism rather than assuming it is only a TCA cofactor.

MOL-25:1.title: Compare a flavin with a pyridine nucleotide
body: Flavins can transfer one or two electrons and commonly serve as tightly associated enzyme cofactors. NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ accept a hydride. NADH mainly carries electrons from energy-yielding reactions, while NADPH often supplies reductive synthesis and antioxidant defense. Both pyridine nucleotides derive from niacin despite their different roles.

MOL-25:2.title: Use methylmalonic acid to separate folate and B₁₂ problems
body: Folate and B₁₂ intersect at methionine synthase, explaining overlapping megaloblastic findings. B₁₂ also serves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which is outside that shared step. Elevated methylmalonic acid therefore points toward B₁₂ dysfunction rather than isolated folate deficiency. Neurologic findings provide additional context.

summary: 11-cis-retinal participates in vision; retinoic acid regulates gene expression. Liver 25-hydroxylation and kidney 1α-hydroxylation produce active calcitriol.
Vitamin E interrupts membrane lipid peroxidation; vitamin K enables γ-carboxylation of selected clotting proteins for calcium-dependent binding.
Distinguish vitamin C-related tissue fragility from vitamin K-related clotting dysfunction; fat malabsorption can affect multiple fat-soluble vitamins.

MOL-26:a-d.title: Separate retinoid signaling, vision and calcium regulation
body: Vitamin A is used in distinct forms. 11-cis-retinal participates in the visual pigment cycle; retinoic acid regulates gene expression and differentiation. Vitamin D is hydroxylated in liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and then in kidney to active calcitriol. Calcitriol supports calcium and phosphate homeostasis, including increased intestinal absorption.

In a dark-adaptation question, focus on the retinal chromophore and the visual cycle. A deficiency can impair vision in dim light. A defect in vitamin D availability or activation instead affects mineral homeostasis and can impair bone mineralization. Remember that a fat-soluble classification explains an absorption similarity, not the biochemical action of each vitamin.
MOL-26:a-d.example: When a question asks about light detection, use retinal. When it asks about calcium balance or impaired mineralization, follow the vitamin D activation sequence and the target tissue.

MOL-26:e-k.title: Separate lipid antioxidant protection from clotting activation
body: Vitamin E helps terminate lipid-peroxidation chain reactions in membranes. Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of selected proteins, including clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. Carboxylation permits calcium-dependent interactions with phospholipid surfaces. Warfarin interferes with vitamin K recycling rather than acting as a direct inhibitor of every clotting factor.

Fat malabsorption can reduce uptake of multiple fat-soluble vitamins, so a common upstream disorder can create distinct downstream effects. Vitamin E deficiency can expose cell membranes to oxidation; vitamin K deficiency can reduce the functional activity of newly made clotting proteins. The modification depends on a reduced vitamin K pool, so blocking its recycling has a delayed effect as existing proteins turn over.
MOL-26:e-k.example: Membrane oxidation and defective coagulation can both produce clinical findings involving blood. Decide whether the mechanism is protection of membrane lipids or post-translational modification of proteins.

MOL-26:0.title: Distinguish vitamin C-related bleeding from a clotting defect
body: Vitamin C supports hydroxylation during collagen synthesis. With deficiency, bleeding can reflect fragile vessel walls and connective tissue. Vitamin K deficiency changes coagulation protein function through impaired γ-carboxylation. Ask whether the key finding is poor tissue integrity or impaired clot formation before assigning the vitamin.

MOL-26:1.title: Name the vitamin D form from its site of formation
body: The liver produces 25-hydroxyvitamin D, commonly used to assess vitamin D status. The kidney produces the hormonally active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Distinguish a storage or status marker from the active hormone. A question about intestinal calcium absorption asks about calcitriol action, even if a different metabolite is measured clinically.

To localize an activation defect, first identify the form named in the question. 25-hydroxyvitamin D has already been through hepatic hydroxylation. Low active hormone despite available precursor can reflect impaired renal activation. The active form acts through a nuclear receptor; it is not simply calcium carried into the blood by vitamin D.

MOL-26:2.title: Use the biochemical target to distinguish A, E and K
body: Retinoids can regulate differentiation or participate in vision, depending on the form. Vitamin E protects membrane lipids against propagating oxidation. Vitamin K enables a specific protein modification required for calcium binding. In a case, translate a symptom into its underlying process before choosing the vitamin.

summary: DNA and RNA polymerases synthesize 5′→3′ by adding to a 3′ end. RNA is complementary to the template and matches the coding strand except U for T.
The ribosome reads mRNA 5′→3′ and makes peptide N-to-C; A/P/E sites handle incoming, peptidyl and exiting tRNAs, with initiator tRNA entering P.
Protein function depends on local interactions, packing and targeting signals. Charged glycosaminoglycans attract water and resist compression; not all are sulfated.

MOL-27:information-review.title: Follow directional information from DNA to protein
body: Track direction at every stage. DNA polymerase extends a growing 3′ end, so DNA is synthesized 5′ to 3′ while its template is read in the opposite direction. RNA polymerase likewise makes RNA 5′ to 3′. The RNA matches the coding strand over the transcribed sequence except for uracil in place of thymine, while being complementary to the template strand.

During translation, the ribosome reads mRNA codons from 5′ to 3′ and grows the peptide from its amino terminus toward its carboxyl terminus. Separate base-pairing direction from peptide synthesis direction in a mixed case.

For a worked strand check, a template written 3′-TAC GGA-5′ gives the RNA 5′-AUG CCU-3′. The corresponding coding strand is 5′-ATG CCT-3′. In a translation question, AUG provides a start context and CCU encodes proline, but a DNA-copying question asks for a DNA strand with thymine. Check the requested product before reusing the same base sequence.

MOL-27:structure-review.title: Connect interaction strength to molecular function
body: A protein can lose function because a substitution disrupts local charge interactions, hydrophobic packing, or an active-site contact. A new covalent bond is not required for a structural change. The effect also depends on location: burying a charged residue can be more disruptive than placing it on a solvent-exposed surface.

Glycosaminoglycans behave differently. Many are highly negatively charged and attract counterions and water, helping hydrated matrices resist compression. Distinguish water retention in extracellular matrix from the hydrophobic effect that helps drive many soluble proteins to fold.

MOL-27:0.title: Identify the strand from its 3′ end and orientation
body: Polymerase adds to a 3′ hydroxyl; the new strand therefore grows 5′ to 3′. The template runs antiparallel. If a template is printed 5′ to 3′, write its complement and reverse it before reporting the product 5′ to 3′. Check the two orientation labels independently of the base letters.

MOL-27:1.title: Trace a tRNA through the ribosome
body: In elongation an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site, the P site holds the peptidyl-tRNA before transfer, and the E site releases a deacylated tRNA. Peptidyl transfer puts the growing chain on the A-site tRNA before translocation moves it to P. The initiator tRNA is an exception because it initially enters the P site.

MOL-27:2.title: Explain how negative charge contributes to matrix mechanics
body: Acidic groups on glycosaminoglycan chains attract cations and water. A hydrated matrix can resist compression as water is displaced and then returns. This differs from tensile reinforcement by collagen. Hyaluronan is an important nonsulfated example, so sulfation alone cannot define the class.

summary: Fed state favors glucose use and storage; fasting uses liver glycogen and increasingly gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids.
Acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle or supports ketogenesis but provides no net glucose carbon in humans. Distinguish tracer labeling from net carbon balance.
NADH carries electrons from fuel oxidation; NADPH supports reductive synthesis and GSH recycling. Glycogen branching and vitamin C-dependent collagen hydroxylation are distinct mechanisms.

MOL-28:carbon-review.title: Follow carbon as fuel use shifts from fed to fasting
body: In the fed state, glucose can be oxidized, stored as glycogen or used to supply carbon for biosynthesis. During early fasting, liver glycogen breakdown helps maintain blood glucose; as glycogen becomes depleted, gluconeogenesis takes a larger share. Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids can contribute net glucose carbon.

Acetyl-CoA can enter the TCA cycle or support ketone production when hepatic conditions favor it. Humans do not convert acetyl-CoA into net glucose carbon through the TCA cycle. Track net carbon rather than assuming any intermediate appearing downstream proves a net pathway.

Compare lactate returning from muscle with acetyl-CoA arriving from fatty-acid oxidation. Lactate can become pyruvate and contribute carbon to glucose. Fatty-acid oxidation supplies energy and acetyl-CoA to support fasting metabolism, but the acetyl group cannot supply net glucose through the TCA cycle. Glycerol from triacylglycerol is a separate carbon source and should not be confused with its fatty-acid chains.

MOL-28:redox-review.title: Choose NADH or NADPH from the task being performed
body: NADH generally carries electrons from fuel oxidation to pathways that regenerate NAD⁺, including mitochondrial electron transport. NADPH supports reductive synthesis and antioxidant defense. The pentose phosphate pathway generates cytosolic NADPH, which glutathione reductase uses to regenerate GSH. These carriers are related chemically but used by different enzyme systems.

When oxidative phosphorylation is impaired, mitochondrial NADH can accumulate because the chain regenerates less NAD⁺. That says little by itself about the cytosolic NADPH supply. In a red-cell oxidative challenge, look instead for PPP generation of NADPH and glutathione recycling. High NADH, high NADPH and high ATP are three distinct statements.
MOL-28:redox-review.example: A cell can have a highly reduced NADH pool after ethanol oxidation while having inadequate NADPH-dependent antioxidant reserve. Name the enzyme and cofactor before interpreting “reducing power.”

MOL-28:0.title: Distinguish tracing a carbon atom from making net glucose
body: Acetyl-CoA adds two carbons to oxaloacetate to form citrate. The cycle regenerates oxaloacetate while releasing two carbons per turn, so acetyl-CoA supplies no net oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis. The two entering carbons need not be the first two released. A tracer can therefore appear in a cycle intermediate even though net conversion to glucose is impossible.

MOL-28:1.title: Connect glycogen branching to rapid fuel mobilization
body: Chain segments use α(1→4) bonds and branches use α(1→6). More branches mean more nonreducing ends, so many phosphorylase molecules can mobilize residues in parallel. Branch removal still requires a distinct debranching mechanism. Recognize whether a question asks about the number of accessible ends or the chemistry of a single branch.

MOL-28:2.title: Connect vitamin C to enzyme function rather than energy production
body: Ascorbate supports the reduced iron state in collagen hydroxylases. The result is proper hydroxylation and collagen stability, not a direct increase in ATP generation. In a combined nutrition case, contrast poor wound healing and fragile connective tissue with a defect in oxidative decarboxylation or a vitamin K-dependent clotting change.
